questions.question: A 'retractile' testis is distinguished from a true undescended testis by the fact that:

options.A: A retractile testis can be manipulated without tension into the base of the scrotum, though it is pulled back up by the cremaster muscle
options.B: A retractile testis is always impalpable
options.C: A retractile testis requires orchidopexy immediately
options.D: There is no meaningful difference between the two

questions.explanation: A retractile testis can be brought down to the base of the scrotum without tension, but is then pulled back up by an overactive cremaster reflex — over time it usually resides permanently in the scrotum, though follow-up is still advised as it can rarely re-ascend and require orchidopexy.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — Undescended Testes
questions.subject: General Surgery & Orthopedics

questions.question: Pyridoxal phosphate is required for the synthesis of delta-aminolevulinic acid, which is the precursor for:

options.A: Heme synthesis
options.B: Cholesterol synthesis
options.C: Glycogen synthesis
options.D: DNA synthesis

questions.explanation: PLP is required for the synthesis of delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA), the key precursor molecule in the heme biosynthesis pathway — linking vitamin B6 status to haemoglobin production.
questions.sourceChapter: Vitamins — Vitamin B6, Biochemical Functions
questions.subject: Biochemistry

questions.question: In the Active Compression Test of O'Brien, pain that is present with the arm pronated (thumb down) but reduced or eliminated with the arm supinated (thumb up) suggests a positive test for:

options.A: A superior labral (SLAP) injury
options.B: A simple rotator cuff strain with no labral involvement
options.C: Carpal tunnel syndrome
options.D: Lateral epicondylitis

questions.explanation: O'Brien's active compression test is positive for a superior labral injury when pain (felt 'inside' the shoulder, not at the AC joint) is produced with the arm pronated, and is reduced or eliminated when the same maneuver is repeated with the arm supinated.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 5: Shoulder — Active Compression Test of O'Brien
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: When a muscle is immobilized after injury, which muscle fiber type atrophies at a FASTER rate, and what is the clinical implication?

options.A: Type II (fast twitch) fibers atrophy faster, so power training should be prioritized immediately
options.B: Type I (slow twitch) fibers atrophy faster, contributing to faster atrophy of antigravity muscles and underscoring the need for early endurance training
options.C: Both fiber types atrophy at exactly the same rate with immobilization
options.D: Immobilization has no effect on muscle fiber composition

questions.explanation: With immobilization, Type I (slow twitch) fibers atrophy faster than Type II (fast twitch) fibers, and there is also a slow-to-fast fiber type conversion with disuse. Since antigravity (postural) muscles rely heavily on Type I fibers, this contributes to their faster rate of atrophy compared to their antagonists — supporting early initiation of endurance-type training after injury or surgery.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Muscle Fiber Atrophy
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: Lesions of the parietal lobe of the NONDOMINANT (typically right) hemisphere in MCA syndrome typically produce which type of deficit?

options.A: Aphasia (language impairment)
options.B: Perceptual deficits such as unilateral neglect, anosognosia, and spatial disorganization
options.C: Complete loss of hearing
options.D: Loss of the sense of smell only

questions.explanation: While dominant (usually left) hemisphere parieto-occipital lesions typically produce aphasia, lesions of the nondominant (usually right) parietal lobe typically produce perceptual deficits: unilateral neglect, anosognosia (denial of deficit), apraxia, and spatial disorganization.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Middle Cerebral Artery Syndrome
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: The law of 'good figure' (or symmetry) in perceptual organization can override the law of similarity when:

options.A: Grouping by similarity alone would not produce a symmetrical, balanced figure, but combining all elements does
options.B: The elements are all completely identical in every way
options.C: There is no visual stimulus present at all
options.D: Good figure and similarity are actually the exact same principle

questions.explanation: When grouping elements purely by similarity (e.g. dots vs. rings) would not create a symmetrical/balanced figure, but using ALL the elements together does produce one (e.g. a six-pointed star), the law of good figure/symmetry tends to win out over the law of similarity.
questions.sourceChapter: Sensory Processes and Perception — Organization in Perception
questions.subject: Psychology

questions.question: During a maximum-effort CONCENTRIC muscle contraction, what happens to the force a muscle can generate as the velocity of shortening increases?

options.A: Force increases continuously with velocity
options.B: Force decreases as the velocity of muscle shortening increases
options.C: Force remains completely constant regardless of velocity
options.D: Force becomes unmeasurable at any velocity above zero

questions.explanation: For a maximal concentric contraction, force output decreases as the velocity of muscle shortening increases — the muscle has less time to develop peak tension at higher shortening velocities. This is opposite to the pattern often seen with eccentric contractions, where force initially rises with velocity before leveling off.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Force-Velocity Relationship
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: Per the criteria described for a 'normal pregnancy', delivery is expected to occur at term (between 38-42 weeks) with a fetal weight of at least:

options.A: 1.0 kg
options.B: 2.5 kg
options.C: 5.0 kg
options.D: Weight is not part of the criteria

questions.explanation: The criteria for a 'normal pregnancy' include delivery of a single baby in good condition at term (38-42 weeks), with a fetal weight of 2.5 kg or more, and with no maternal complications — making 'normal pregnancy' technically a retrospective classification.
questions.sourceChapter: Antenatal Care — Aims and Objectives
questions.subject: OBGY

questions.question: Which of the following correctly distinguishes tendinitis, tenosynovitis, and tendinosis?

options.A: Tendinitis is inflammation of a tendon; tenosynovitis is inflammation of the synovial membrane covering a tendon; tendinosis is degeneration of the tendon from repetitive microtrauma (not primarily inflammatory)
options.B: All three terms describe exactly the same pathological process
options.C: Tendinosis is an acute inflammatory condition, more severe than tendinitis
options.D: Tenosynovitis only affects ligaments, never tendons

questions.explanation: Tendinitis is inflammation of a tendon (possibly with scarring or calcium deposits); tenosynovitis is inflammation of the synovial membrane covering a tendon; tendinosis is tendon degeneration from repetitive microtrauma, distinct from the acute inflammatory conditions.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 10: Soft Tissue Injury, Repair, and Management — Soft Tissue Lesions
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: In periodized training, the 'competition' phase is generally characterized by:

options.A: Lower loads and the highest number of repetitions and sets
options.B: Higher loads (peaking just prior to competition), with fewer exercises per session and reduced volume compared to the preparation phase
options.C: Complete rest with no exercise
options.D: Only aerobic exercise, no resistance training

questions.explanation: In periodized training, the competition phase uses higher loads peaking just before competition, along with fewer exercises per session and decreased repetitions/sets compared to the earlier preparation phase, which uses lower loads and higher volume.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Periodization and Variation of Training
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: Although prolactin levels are high throughout pregnancy, actual milk secretion does not begin until around the 3rd-4th postpartum day. What explains this delay?

options.A: Prolactin has no role in milk secretion at all
options.B: High circulating estrogen and progesterone during pregnancy make breast tissue unresponsive to prolactin; their withdrawal after delivery allows prolactin to act
options.C: The breasts are not anatomically ready until several days after birth
options.D: Oxytocin blocks prolactin receptors until labour is complete

questions.explanation: During pregnancy, the high circulating levels of estrogen and progesterone keep the fully-developed mammary glands unresponsive to prolactin, holding milk secretion in abeyance despite high prolactin levels. Once these steroids fall sharply after delivery, prolactin is free to begin its secretory (lactogenic) action.
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Physiology of Lactation, Lactogenesis
questions.subject: OBGY

questions.question: A patient with damage to the RIGHT parietal association cortex draws a clock face but only completes the right half, leaving the left side blank, and is unaware anything is missing. This phenomenon is known as:

options.A: Wernicke's aphasia
options.B: Contralateral neglect
options.C: Prosopagnosia
options.D: Broca's aphasia

questions.explanation: Contralateral neglect is a classic sign of right parietal association cortex damage: patients ignore the left side of space and their own body (the side opposite/contralateral to the damaged hemisphere), often while denying anything is wrong.
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Parietal-Lobe Association Cortex
questions.subject: Psychology

questions.question: Per Snyder's classification, a Type II SLAP lesion — described as the most common type — is characterised by:

options.A: A superior labrum that is markedly frayed but with intact attachments
options.B: A small tear with instability of the labral-biceps complex
options.C: A bucket-handle tear that may displace into the joint, with the labral-biceps attachment intact
options.D: A bucket-handle tear extending to the biceps tendon, allowing it to sublux into the joint

questions.explanation: Snyder's classification describes Type I (frayed superior labrum, intact attachments), Type II (small tear with labral-biceps complex instability — the most common type), Type III (bucket-handle tear, labral-biceps attachment intact), and Type IV (bucket-handle tear extending to the biceps tendon, allowing subluxation).
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 5: Shoulder — Tests for Labral Tears, SLAP Classification
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: How are night terrors (pavor nocturnus) distinguished from nightmares?

options.A: Night terrors occur during REM sleep and are clearly remembered; nightmares occur during NREM sleep and are forgotten
options.B: Night terrors occur during Stage 4 NREM sleep early in the night with complete amnesia; nightmares occur during REM sleep, usually later in the night, and are clearly remembered
options.C: There is no real difference between the two conditions
options.D: Both occur exclusively in adults, never in children

questions.explanation: Night terrors are a Stage 4 NREM parasomnia occurring in the first third of the night, with autonomic arousal (tachycardia, sweating) and complete amnesia for the event on waking. Nightmares, by contrast, occur during REM sleep (more common in the last third of the night) and are vividly and clearly remembered.
questions.sourceBook: Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry
questions.sourceChapter: Sleep Disorders — Parasomnias, Stage 4 Sleep Disorders
questions.subject: Psychiatry

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: Because of accommodation, which type of current change is MORE effective at initiating a nerve impulse: a sudden change, or a gradual one?

options.A: A sudden change in current is more effective than a gradual one
options.B: A gradual change is always more effective
options.C: Both are exactly equally effective in all cases
options.D: Neither a sudden nor gradual change can ever initiate an impulse

questions.explanation: Because the nerve accommodates (adapts) to slowly changing conditions, a current that rises or falls suddenly is more effective at initiating an impulse than one that changes gradually, since gradual change gives the nerve time to accommodate before the threshold is reached.
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Accommodation
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: A SLAP lesion (Superior Labrum, Anterior and Posterior) involves detachment of the labrum at approximately which clock-face position, and is often caused by what mechanism?

options.A: 10 to 2 o'clock position; often from a FOOSH injury or during deceleration in throwing
options.B: 3 to 7 o'clock position; only from anterior dislocation
options.C: 6 o'clock position exclusively; from a direct blow to the shoulder
options.D: SLAP lesions never have an identifiable mechanism

questions.explanation: A SLAP lesion involves detachment of the labrum from roughly the 10 to 2 o'clock position, often occurring from a FOOSH (fall on outstretched hand) injury or during the deceleration phase of throwing; if the biceps tendon also detaches, the superior glenohumeral ligament support is lost and the shoulder becomes unstable.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 5: Shoulder — Tests for Labral Tears
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: In a patient with a spinal cord injury who lacks active control of the back extensors, why might a therapist deliberately allow mild hypomobility to develop in the low back extensors while still fully stretching the hamstrings?

options.A: To create a stable, slightly shortened structure the patient can lean into for trunk support during long-term sitting
options.B: Because the back extensors cannot physically be stretched
options.C: To prevent contractures developing in the hamstrings only
options.D: Because stretching the trunk has no clinical value in this population

questions.explanation: This illustrates 'selective stretching': deliberately allowing some hypomobility in muscles the patient cannot actively control (like the back extensors after a thoracic/cervical spinal cord injury) gives them a stable structure to lean into for trunk stability while sitting, while the hamstrings are kept flexible enough for dressing and transfers.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 4: Stretching for Impaired Mobility — Selective Stretching
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Exercise Therapy

questions.question: The D-dimer test has high sensitivity but low specificity for pulmonary embolism. What does this mean in practice?

options.A: A positive D-dimer confirms pulmonary embolism definitively
options.B: A negative D-dimer helps rule out pulmonary embolism, but a positive result does not confirm it — it only means the disease has not been excluded
options.C: The D-dimer test is useless in clinical practice
options.D: High sensitivity and low specificity mean the test is always accurate regardless of result

questions.explanation: A highly sensitive test detects most true disease (few false negatives), so a negative result is reassuring and helps exclude the disease. But low specificity means many people without the disease will still test positive (false positives) — so a raised D-dimer does not confirm pulmonary embolism, it simply means it cannot yet be excluded, prompting further imaging.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Clinical Decision Making — Interpreting Test Results
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: In fat necrosis due to acute pancreatitis, free fatty acids released from ruptured adipocytes combine with calcium to form:

options.A: Calcium soaps (saponification)
options.B: Haemosiderin
options.C: Lipofuscin granules
options.D: Amyloid deposits

questions.explanation: In fat necrosis, liberated pancreatic lipases cause hydrolysis of adipocytes, releasing free fatty acids which complex with calcium to form calcium soaps — a process called saponification, giving the necrotic foci their firm, chalky-white gross appearance.
questions.sourceChapter: Cell Injury, Cellular Adaptations and Cellular Ageing — Fat Necrosis
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: The Gibbs-Donnan membrane equilibrium describes what happens when a membrane permeable to some ions separates two solutions, one of which also contains a non-diffusible (non-penetrating) ion such as a protein anion. What is the key consequence?

options.A: All ions distribute exactly equally on both sides regardless of the non-diffusible ion
options.B: The diffusible ions distribute asymmetrically at equilibrium — the diffusible cation concentration is higher on the side containing the non-penetrating anion
options.C: The non-diffusible ion eventually crosses the membrane too, given enough time
options.D: No electrical potential difference develops across the membrane

questions.explanation: When a non-diffusible anion (like a protein) is confined to one side, the freely diffusible ions (like K+ and Cl-) redistribute asymmetrically at equilibrium to maintain electrical neutrality and equal ion products on both sides — the diffusible cation ends up more concentrated on the side with the trapped anion. This asymmetry is the Gibbs-Donnan equilibrium and contributes to the resting membrane potential.
questions.sourceChapter: The Membrane Potentials — Gibbs-Donnan Membrane Equilibrium
questions.subject: Physiology
